newsitem.title: USA: Miami oversight board says budget needs more work.
newsitem.headline: Miami oversight board says budget needs more work.

text.p: A state oversight board sent Miami's five-year bailout plan back for revisions Monday, saying it lacked specifics on how the city planned to erase deficits in 1999 through 2001.
"You've got millions of dollars of deficits out there that the plan doesn't address," board member Cynthia Curry told City Manager Ed Marquez and Mayor Joe Carrollo.
There was no formal vote on whether to accept the budget, but "You can see where the votes are on this board," said Lt. Gov. Buddy MacKay, who chairs the oversight board.
"The board feels that we've got to be presented with a plan that balances over four to five years," MacKay said.

The plan eliminated a $68 million deficit for fiscal 1997 through wage concessions, cuts in services and one-time revenues. It balances in 1998, but has growing deficits of up to $42 million in 1999 through 2001.

Board members and their staff said the plan did not meet the requirements of the intergovernmental agreement that created the board to guide Miami's fiscal recovery. The contract said the five-year plan "should eliminate all known deficits" and present a strucutrally balanced budget.
Marquez said the city had several alternatives to eliminate the deficits, including privatization of some services, new fees, millage increases and cuts in services.
The board asked the city to list each alternative, provide detailed revenue projections for each, and get a commitment from the city commission to implement them if necessary.

"You don't have to make a decision (immediately) on which alternative you'll take," board member Mariea Camila Leiva said. "You can have four or five alternatives. But you need to quantify your alternatives."

City officials have been loathe to do that. They already approved an unpopular new fire-resecue service fee and fear the impact that any more tax hikes or service cuts would have on the upcoming referendum on whether Miami should be dissolved and merged into the Metro-Dade County government.
"We are going to have to explain to the people why they should vote for a government that is taxing them to death," Vice Mayor Tomas Regalado said.
"It's a self-fulfilling nightmare," Marquez said. "If we're here honestly trying to get this city out of the mess, we've got to move gradually."

The referendum was forced by disgruntled residents who started a petition campaign in protest of a city hall corruption scandal and the city's financial woes. The commission has until Wednesday to draft the ballot language and until September 4 to hold the referendum.

Regalado asked the board to give the city until the current fiscal year ends September 30 to refine its budget. The board, which rejected a similar request earlier this month, tabled the request without discussion.
The board has until May 1 to approve or reject the budget., Gov. Lawton Chiles appointed the board and could take over the city, although he has said that would be an absolute last resort.
